I am sixty-three years old and have worked this land for forty years. My husband and I are the only ones left at home — our children are in the city — and he takes odd jobs away from the farm when he can, so I must plan for my own two hands. We have 12.4 mu and a well that gives steady water. I know every plot by feel.

I will keep 10 mu in the wheat-maize rotation that has fed us for decades. It is reliable, the machines from the village cooperative help with harvest, and I can manage the schedule. The remaining 2.4 mu I will plant to cotton. I would plant more if I were younger, but picking cotton is back-breaking work and there is nobody to help me carry the sacks. Two and a half mu is enough to bring in cash without breaking my body.

My winter wheat is already in the ground from last autumn. I sowed an improved variety from the township supply shop — not the most expensive seed, but the one my neighbors trust. This spring I will top-dress with urea when the wheat greens up, and I will irrigate three times from the well: once at revival, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. I do not spread as much fertilizer as the young men with big farms; too much nitrogen makes the wheat grow tall and fall over in a storm, and I have learned that from hard experience. I will spray a couple of times for bugs and disease, and once for weeds. I expect about 500 kg per mu if the weather holds.

After the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant hybrid maize straight into the stubble without ploughing. There is no time to waste in the summer heat, and no-tillage saves diesel and labor. I will put down compound fertilizer with the seed and maybe top-dress once if the leaves look pale. Two irrigations should be enough — one when it is tasseling and another at grain fill — because summer usually brings some rain. I will spray for weeds, borers, and rust. Hybrid maize should give me around 550 kg per mu.

For cotton, I will rotary-till the 2.4 mu in April and plant improved Bt cotton seed. Cotton needs careful water, so I will irrigate three times: at flowering, at peak boll-set, and once more before the bolls open. I will spray eight times through the season for aphids, bollworms, and leaf spot — cotton is fussy and I cannot afford to let the pests take it. I expect about 280 kg of seed cotton per mu, which the buyer from the county town will purchase in the autumn.
